6 questions. Click an answer to check it: you will see right away whether it is correct, with a short explanation. Nothing is saved.

::: {.sb-quiz-q data-answer="1"}
**1.** What does Bayes' theorem allow us to compute?

::: {.sb-quiz-options}
- $P(A \cap B)$ from $P(A)$ and $P(B)$
- $P(A|B)$ from $P(B|A)$, $P(A)$ and $P(B)$
- The mean of a distribution
- The correlation between two variables
:::

::: {.sb-quiz-explain}
$P(A|B) = \dfrac{P(B|A)\,P(A)}{P(B)}$. In classification: the probability of a class given the features, from the probability of the features within each class.
:::
:::

::: {.sb-quiz-q data-answer="1"}
**2.** Why is Naive Bayes called *naive*?

::: {.sb-quiz-options}
- Because it is a simple model for beginners
- Because it assumes that the features are independent within each class
- Because it ignores the prior probabilities
- Because it only works with two classes
:::

::: {.sb-quiz-explain}
The independence assumption is rarely true, but it makes the model very fast and it often works surprisingly well, for instance on text.
:::
:::

::: {.sb-quiz-q data-answer="1"}
**3.** What does `GaussianNB` assume about each numeric feature?

::: {.sb-quiz-options}
- That it is categorical
- That it follows a normal distribution within each class
- That it is between 0 and 1
- That it is standardized
:::

::: {.sb-quiz-explain}
Gaussian Naive Bayes estimates a mean and a variance per feature and per class. Other variants exist for counts (`MultinomialNB`, e.g. word counts) and for binary features (`BernoulliNB`).
:::
:::

::: {.sb-quiz-q data-answer="2"}
**4.** A test detects a disease present in 1% of the population. It is positive for 90% of the sick people and 5% of the healthy people. You test positive: what is the probability that you are sick?

::: {.sb-quiz-options}
- 90%
- 50%
- About 15%
- 5%
:::

::: {.sb-quiz-explain}
$P(\text{sick}|+) = \dfrac{0.9 \times 0.01}{0.9 \times 0.01 + 0.05 \times 0.99} \approx 0.15$. Most positive tests come from the many healthy people: the prior probability matters.
:::
:::

::: {.sb-quiz-q data-answer="1"}
**5.** In the fraud exercise, Naive Bayes finds no fraud with the raw columns, but works well with the engineered features. What does it show?

::: {.sb-quiz-options}
- Naive Bayes is a bad model
- The features matter more than the choice of the model
- The raw columns contain errors
- Fraud can't be predicted
:::

::: {.sb-quiz-explain}
The time between sign-up and purchase and the number of accounts per device carry almost all the information. With them, even the simplest model is close to a random forest.
:::
:::

::: {.sb-quiz-q data-answer="1"}
**6.** In fraud detection, what is a false negative?

::: {.sb-quiz-options}
- A legitimate customer flagged as a fraud
- A fraud that is not detected
- A fraud correctly detected
- A legitimate purchase accepted
:::

::: {.sb-quiz-explain}
False negatives cost money (the fraud goes through); false positives cost customer satisfaction (a legitimate customer is blocked). The decision threshold balances the two.
:::
:::

::: {.sb-quiz-score}
